source.title: P-DIFF: Learning Classifier with Noisy Labels based on Probability Difference Distributions
source.authors: Wei Hu; Qi-Hao Zhao; Yang-Yu Huang; Fan Zhang

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; no material cutoff or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates classifiers across several synthetic label-noise rates and reports test accuracy, a conceptual test of noisy-label generalization. It does not report training error on random labels.
record.gate_note: The paper varies label-noise type and rate and reports test accuracy in Table V. It does not report training error for those runs. No rows are included for cited prior-work findings, training-time comparisons among methods, or P-DIFF’s probability-difference analyses because they do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The Normal baselines provide an own-result test of V4's test-error trend across corruption rates on four datasets. They do not establish perfect training-set fitting. The remaining experiments primarily evaluate noise mitigation; V6 is invoked from prior work rather than independently tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they present P-DIFF as a simple, effective noisy-label training method and claim advantages over compared sample-selection approaches in classification and computational efficiency. This is their overall claim, not universal dominance in every table entry.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces P-DIFF, a sample-selection and reweighting training paradigm for noisy labels; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test accuracy varies with dataset, noise type, and noise rate.

fits_no_version.finding: P-DIFF improves noisy-label test accuracy through sample selection; its distribution analyses evaluate selection and noise estimation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probability-difference-based sample selection can improve classification under label noise.

record.problems: The claim-relevant table reports test accuracy but not training error. Its synthetic corruption settings are symmetry and pair flipping; they do not establish completely random labels or chance-level test error. The text does not specify the architecture separately for each Table V result beyond describing the experimental use of 9-layer and ResNet-101 CNNs.
record.rows_left_out: Table V also reports Clean and competing-method columns. They were omitted because they are not the classic softmax baseline used here to examine the claim’s generalization pattern; cited O2U-Net results are explicitly from its original paper.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases; Table VII compares methods at one corruption rate.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fitting throughout corruption; the zero-to-all corruption trajectory and chance endpoint; direct evidence that remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized. Sparse test-accuracy comparisons cannot establish smoothness between measured rates.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and of their removal on true-label generalization.

Unmodified training dynamics demonstrating real patterns learned before noisy labels. The cited Noise-Adaption premise and P-DIFF's deliberate sample filtering do not independently establish this order.

record.verdict_notes: All twenty extracted accuracy values match Table V. The row states remain cannot_determine for V4's joint claim; the support labels concern only its directly measured test-error component. Table V's Clean column trains on the clean subset, so it is not a zero-corruption baseline using the full training set. Missing training-error measurements are untested evidence, not missing extracted results.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling experiment or training-error result is reported.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels, or convergence rate as corruption increases.
No shuffled-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

Test accuracy is reported across noise types and rates, but the study does not report whether training error remains perfect or whether test error rises steadily toward chance. The corrupted labels use symmetry or pair flipping, not a fully random assignment.
No comparison of explicit regularization or data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The paper cites the Noise-Adaption phenomenon and Arpit et al.; it does not test whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy labels.

relationships.condition: Test-error component only: Normal training with symmetry flipping at 20%, 40%, and 80%, across all four datasets.
relationships.reason: R1–R3, R6–R8, R11–R13, and R16–R18 show successively lower test accuracy as corruption increases; this supports the measured degradation trend, without establishing the full training-fit claim.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy decreased successively with increasing symmetric corruption across all four datasets.

relationships.condition: Test-error component only: Normal training with structured pair flipping at 10% versus 45%, across all four datasets.
relationships.reason: R4–R5, R9–R10, R14–R15, and R19–R20 show lower test accuracy at 45% than 10%; these two-point comparisons support degradation under pair noise only.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy was lower at 45% pair corruption than at 10% across all four datasets.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
